deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's sieve table in E283. For each a from 754 to 811 it lists the prime divisors of a^2+1 that are below about 1000. Any odd prime divisor p of a^2+1 satisfies p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Euler finds these by sieving: for each such p he takes a root r of x^2 ≡ -1 (mod p) and marks every a ≡ ±r (mod p). Factor 2 appears exactly when a is odd. Factor 5 appears exactly when a ≡ 2 or 3 (mod 5). A blank entry (here a = 760, 764, 780, 784) means a^2+1 has no prime factor below 1000. For a < 1000 that factor bound is at least √(a^2+1), so a blank certifies that a^2+1 is prime. An entry '2' alone means (a^2+1)/2 is prime. When the listed factors do not exhaust a^2+1, the leftover cofactor is a prime above 1000. Examples: 754^2+1 = 97·5861, 755^2+1 = 2·257·1109, 756^2+1 = 521·1097. The table is the tool for the paper's goal: certifying large primes (up to about 10^6) of the form a^2+1, (a^2+1)/2 and their cofactors without trial division. Spot checks against the scan all hold:

- 811^2+1 = 2·13·41·617
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the entries spot-checked (about 20 of 58).
At a = 771 the factors are printed out of order ('277. 29'). This looks like 29 was added after the main sieve, but the factorization is correct.

ideas.what: Sieve table of the small prime divisors of a^2+1, built from the roots of x^2 ≡ -1 mod p, used to certify primality of a^2+1, (a^2+1)/2 and large cofactors
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic-polynomial sieve; tables of factors of n^2+1 (cf. Cunningham-type tables)
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii 9 (1764). The well-known slip in this paper, listing 1000009 as prime, was corrected by Euler himself later.

ideas.what: Odd prime divisors of a^2+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) (structural fact underlying the table)
ideas.modern_name: Fermat–Euler theorem on divisors of sums of two squares
